result.summary: Fragments of the Astronomy give the names of the Pleiades and Hyades, and tell how Callisto, Arcas and Orion became constellations. Orion's story covers his blinding, healing, death by a scorpion, and his work at Peloris.

scenes.title: Names of Pleiades and Hyades
scenes.summary: Quoted lines name the Pleiades as daughters of Atlas, with Maia bearing Hermes, and list the Hyades, whom Zeus made stars.

scenes.title: Callisto and Arcas
scenes.summary: Callisto is seduced by Zeus, turned into a bear by Artemis, and nearly killed by her son before Zeus makes her a constellation. Arcas becomes Bootes, and Lycaon serves Zeus a butchered babe.
scenes.stakes: Callisto risks death for entering the forbidden precinct of Zeus.

scenes.title: Orion's Wanderings and Death
scenes.summary: Orion outrages Merope, is blinded by Oenopion, healed by Helius, and killed by Earth's scorpion in Crete. Zeus sets him among the stars.
scenes.stakes: Orion loses his sight and finally his life.

scenes.title: Orion at Peloris
scenes.summary: Hesiod says Orion piled up the promontory at Peloris, then settled in Euboea and became a star.

alias_notes.explanation: The Astronomy's spelling of the Pleiades, doves in Greek.
Arcas is identified with the constellation Bootes, the Bear-warden.

analysis.text: Constellations are explained as rewards or memorials for mortals, often after transgression and suffering.
The Astronomy survives only in quotations by later writers, and its attribution to Hesiod was doubted even in antiquity.

legacy.text: The myths of Callisto and Orion became the standard explanations of Ursa Major and Orion in later Greek and Roman astronomy and poetry.

fun_facts.text: Athenaeus doubts that the poem is really by Hesiod, writing 'forsooth' in the translation.

language_notes.text: "Forsooth" is an archaic, sarcastic word meaning "in truth"; the writer doubts that Hesiod really wrote The Astronomy.
Peleiades means "doves"; the writer notes this form for the Pleiades, the star cluster whose rising and setting marked seasons.
The Graces were goddesses of beauty and charm, so the Hyades are praised as being as lovely as them.
The "forbidden precinct of Zeus" was a sacred enclosure on Mount Lycaeum in Arcadia; any who entered it were said to be put to death.
Bootes means "ox-driver" or herdsman; "Bear-warden" refers to his place in the sky beside the Bear.
"Outraged" here means sexually violated; the text states he was drunk when he did so.
"Close" means an enclosed sacred area, here a precinct dedicated to Poseidon.

context_notes.text: Atlas was the Titan who held up the sky. His seven daughters were the Pleiades, and Maia was the mother of Hermes by Zeus.
The Hyades were a star cluster whose rising was linked with rain; the name was often tied to the root for "rain".
Lycaon is the Arcadian king in the myth who tested Zeus by serving him human flesh, usually said to be punished for it.
Hephaestus was the smith god, and Lemnos was an island sacred to him.
Peloris is the cape in northeastern Sicily, near the strait separating Sicily from Italy.

literary_notes.text: Callisto is saved by the god who caused her ruin, and the constellation name memorializes her misfortune rather than relieving it.
Orion's boast of killing every beast is answered by Earth sending a single scorpion, a fitting and proportionate punishment.
The story explains why Orion and the scorpion appear as constellations, turning a death into a lasting memorial in the sky.
